lessons.title: Expected goals (xG)
lessons.objective: You can explain xG in plain English.

payload.prompt: What does xG measure?

options.text: The actual goals scored in a match
The quality of shots, not the luck
How many shots a team takes

explanation.correct: Exactly. xG is about shot quality and probability, not whether it actually went in. It strips out finishing luck.
explanation.incorrect: xG is expected goals: a probability score for each shot based on angle, distance and situation, independent of whether it went in.
explanation.sayThisLine: The data says we had more quality chances even though we lost one-nil.

payload.prompt: A team wins 3-1 but had 1.2 xG. Unlucky or lucky?

explanation.correct: Right. Scoring 3 from 1.2 xG means they were clinical and lucky: they converted chances at a rate well above the model's predictions.
explanation.incorrect: They had only 1.2 xG but scored 3, so they exceeded the expected value by about 1.8 goals. That's a huge overperformance.
explanation.sayThisLine: We finished clinical today, turned half-chances into goals.

statement.speaker: Leo
statement.text: We lost 1-0 but won the xG 2.1 to 0.3.

payload.question: What is he saying?

options.text: His team played worse than the score shows
His team created better chances but luck went the other way
xG predicts the team will win next time
His team should have won based on the quality of chances

payload.translation: By shot quality and position, his team created chances worth 2.1 goals while the opponent's chances were worth only 0.3. The actual 1-0 loss doesn't reflect who played better.

followUps.line: Did your keeper have to make a crucial save?
followUps.why: Asks about the defensive moment, not the stat.

followUps.line: What should you have done differently in the second half?
followUps.why: Focuses on what was in their control.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: xG is a supporting fact, not a prediction. Luck evens out over a season, but one match can be decided by a single moment.

payload.prompt: Match the stat to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The probability that a shot becomes a goal, based on angle, distance and defensive pressure.
A number that summarizes how dangerous a team's chances were in a match.
Scoring more goals than xG predicted, usually unsustainable over time.

explanation.summary: xG isolates chance quality from finishing. A team outperforming its xG is running hot.
explanation.sayThisLine: We were clinical, the striker finished everything on offer.

payload.prompt: Complete the insight.
payload.template: A team losing 2-0 with 3.5 xG was {{performance}}, and {{outlook}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Scoring only 2 from 3.5 xG means they underperformed, and underperformance tends to reverse.
explanation.incorrect: Underperformance (low goals from high xG) usually corrects over time as a team's actual finishing rate returns to normal.

payload.prompt: A player has many assists but low xA. What does that mean?

options.text: He is not creating chances for others
His teammates are clinical finishers
He plays too defensively

explanation.correct: Exactly. He's setting up low-xG chances that his team is converting at a high rate. High assists, low xA = efficient teammates.
explanation.incorrect: Low xA (expected assists) means the chances he's creating aren't high-quality on paper, but his teammates are finishing them anyway.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's finding the strikers in good positions, they're doing the rest.

statement.speaker: Zara
statement.text: His xA is great even if the strikers keep missing.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The striker is not good
He creates dangerous chances even though they aren't being finished
The team should trade the striker
His assists will improve when strikers get form

payload.translation: The data shows he's threading high-quality passes into dangerous positions; the strikers' finishing is the issue, not his creation.

followUps.line: Does he take risks with his passes?
Who should your team bring in to finish chances?
followUps.why: Discusses the team need, not the player's stats.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: xA is how good the chance was, not how good the assist looked. A back-heel to an open striker counts more than a fifty-yard curler into the corner.

payload.prompt: A 20-yard pass from defence into the attacking third. Progressive pass?

scene.alt: A defender passes the ball forward from the defensive third to a teammate in the attacking third, moving it significantly closer to goal.

explanation.correct: Yes. A progressive pass meaningfully moves the ball towards the opponent's goal. This does.
explanation.incorrect: A pass that advances the ball significantly towards goal is progressive. A 20-yard leap forward definitely is.
explanation.sayThisLine: One touch, one pass, and we're in the attacking third.

payload.prompt: A player has 5 assists and 3.2 xA. Which is true?

options.text: He is overperforming; strikers are finishing above their quality
The stat is wrong
He is creating low-quality chances

explanation.correct: Right. He's assisted 5 goals from chances that the model valued at 3.2 goals. His strikers are converting at above-normal rates.
explanation.incorrect: xA is based on the quality of the chances he creates. More assists than xA means his teammates are finishing better than expected.

payload.prompt: Match the creation term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The sum of the xG of shots that result from a player's passes, measuring chance creation quality.
A pass that moves the ball meaningfully closer to the opponent's goal.
A precise pass that splits defenders and puts a teammate through on goal.

explanation.summary: Chance creation is measured by the quality of shots from your passes, not just the number of assists.
explanation.sayThisLine: He threads through balls into dangerous areas, the finishers just have to put them away.

payload.prompt: Lower PPDA means the team is doing what?

options.text: Playing more passes overall
Pressing harder, forcing fewer passes
Defending deeper

explanation.correct: Exactly. PPDA is passes allowed per defensive action. Low PPDA means the defense acts often, interrupting the opponent's build-up.
explanation.incorrect: PPDA measures how many passes the opponent gets before a defensive action (tackle, interception, foul) stops them. Low = more pressing.
explanation.sayThisLine: We're in their face, not giving them space to settle.

payload.prompt: Estimate: heavy press, low PPDA. What range?

explanation.correct: Right. A heavy press sits under 8 PPDA, often 6 or lower, meaning an action every few passes.
explanation.incorrect: Heavy pressing teams force a defensive action very frequently. PPDA of 6 or below indicates relentless pressure.
explanation.sayThisLine: We're winning the ball every five or six passes, they can't build out.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: Their PPDA is under eight, that's a heavy press.

payload.question: What is the coach saying?

options.text: The opponent has 8 players
The opponent is defending deep
The opponent is pressing aggressively throughout the pitch
They intercept the ball frequently

payload.translation: The opponent forces a defensive action within every eight passes or so, meaning they are pressing hard and not giving time on the ball.

followUps.line: How do you counter that kind of press?
Can they sustain that intensity for ninety minutes?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: PPDA tells you intensity; it doesn't tell you if the press is effective. A high PPDA might mean the team is deep, not soft.

payload.prompt: A team has a 10+ PPDA. Most likely they are doing what?

options.text: Pressing high and compact
Sitting deep and defending blocks
Playing long balls

explanation.correct: Right. High PPDA means the opponent gets many passes before an action, suggesting a low block that lets them build out.
explanation.incorrect: PPDA above 10 indicates a passive defensive shape that allows the opponent to move the ball comfortably before challenging.
explanation.sayThisLine: They're camped in their half, we can build out from the back.

payload.prompt: Complete the press assessment.
payload.template: PPDA under 6 means {{intensity}}, while PPDA over 11 means {{defense}}.

explanation.correct: Correct. Low PPDA = pressing team; high PPDA = sitting-deep team.
explanation.incorrect: PPDA inversely measures pressing intensity. Under 6 is relentless, over 11 is reactive.

lessons.title: Possession is not control
lessons.objective: You can explain why possession can mislead.

payload.prompt: 60% possession, no shots on target. What does that suggest?

options.text: The team with possession played well
Possession itself does not guarantee dangerous play
The goalkeeper made great saves

explanation.correct: Exactly. You can have the ball without creating danger. Possession is territory; shots are threat.
explanation.incorrect: High possession but no shots on target means the team was passing sideways and backwards, not attacking.
explanation.sayThisLine: Sixty percent possession but not one shot on target.

statement.speaker: Commentator
statement.text: We dominated possession all night but they caught us on the break.

payload.question: What went wrong?

options.text: The team did not control the tempo of the match
The opponent's defence was too good
Having the ball does not protect against counterattacks
Possession guarantees you will score

payload.translation: Holding the ball often means little if you are not creating danger or dictating the pace. The opponent waited and struck when the team was exposed.

followUps.line: Did you press them too high?
How did they transition so quickly?
followUps.why: Focuses on what the opponent did.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The best teams have both: they control possession and create chances. Low possession can work if a team is clinical on the break.

payload.prompt: Team A: 55% possession, 12 shots on target. Team B: 45% possession, 8 shots. Team A more dangerous?

scene.alt: Two teams' statistics shown side by side: Team A with more passes and possession, Team B with fewer passes but more efficient shooting.

explanation.correct: Right. More possession does not guarantee more danger. Team A's shots outnumber Team B's, so Team A is more threatening.
explanation.incorrect: Possession alone is not the measure. Team A took more shots on target, which is the better indicator of attacking threat.
explanation.sayThisLine: They had less ball but sharper in the box.

payload.prompt: Which team 'controls the tempo'?

options.text: The team passing backwards more
The team dictating when and where the game is played
The team with higher possession

explanation.correct: Yes. Tempo control is about rhythm and dictation, not possession percentage. A team playing slow and methodical controls it differently than one playing fast breaks.
explanation.incorrect: Controlling the tempo means setting the pace and intensity of the match, not just holding the ball.

payload.prompt: Match the concept to its definition.

pairs.definition: The proportion of time a team holds the ball; it says nothing about what they do with it.
Dictating the pace and rhythm of the match: whether play is slow, direct, methodical or chaotic.
The likelihood and quality of shots and chances created, independent of possession.

explanation.summary: Possession is a resource. Threat is what you do with it. Tempo is how you control the rhythm.
explanation.sayThisLine: We had the ball but they set the pace, and it suited them.

lessons.title: Over- and underperforming
lessons.objective: You can explain why finishing streaks fade.

payload.prompt: A striker is scoring 5 goals from 2.0 xG. What usually happens next?

options.text: He keeps scoring at that rate
His finishing regresses towards expected levels
His xG will drop to match his goals

explanation.correct: Right. Overperformance is usually unsustainable. Regression to the mean says his finishing will likely drop towards his xG level.
explanation.incorrect: Extreme overperformance typically regresses. A striker scoring 5 from 2.0 xG is running very hot and will likely cool down.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's overperforming his xG so it won't last.

facts.label: Season average
facts.value: 0.8 xG per game, 0.7 goals per game

facts.label: Offer
facts.value: Sell for record fee or keep for the title run

options.text: Sell for the record fee
options.consequence: You sell at peak value, but lose your best finisher when form regresses as expected. Title hopes fade.
options.considerations: Overperformance is temporary, but losing your striker mid-season is costly.

options.text: Keep him and chase the title
options.consequence: He regresses but is still above his season average and your team stays competitive. You benefit from his relative overperformance.
options.considerations: Expect his goal tally to drop closer to 0.7-0.8 per game, but at that level he still contributes.

options.text: Loan him out to build confidence
options.consequence: You remove the player from pressure, but also from your title challenge. Works if you have depth.
options.considerations: Risky mid-season when you need production.

payload.expertNote: A smart team sells strikers at peak overperformance, but a team fighting for a title keeps them. You know form will dip; the question is whether you need him.

statement.speaker: Pundit
statement.text: He's underperforming his xG, that's when you back the player to turn it around.

payload.question: What is the pundit saying?

options.text: The player is not skilled
The player will likely improve as finishing regresses to normal
The player should be sold immediately
His xG is higher than his goal tally, so regression helps him

payload.translation: When a striker is scoring below his expected level, the stats suggest he will score more in the future as his luck improves.

followUps.line: How many games until he's back to normal?
followUps.why: Regression takes time, and you're asking about the timeline.

followUps.line: Has his xG stayed the same?
followUps.why: Distinguishes between slump and loss of form.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Underperformance is encouraging news: the player is getting chances, just not finishing them. Overperformance is the opposite warning sign.

payload.prompt: Over a season, most strikers' goal totals move towards their xG. Over how long?

options.text: Within one week
Over 10-15 matches
Regression is instant

explanation.correct: Correct. Regression to the mean takes a full sample size of games, usually 10-15 matches or more.
explanation.incorrect: Regression is not instant. It takes multiple games for a player's actual finishing to reflect their quality of chances.

payload.prompt: Complete the forward's profile.
payload.template: A forward with 1.2 xG per game but 1.8 goals per game is {{status}}, and this {{sustainability}}.

options: means his xG is too low

explanation.correct: Right. Outscoring your xG is great short-term, but it regresses. Expect his goal tally to drop towards 1.2.
explanation.incorrect: Overperformance (more goals than xG) usually reverses. Over time, actual scoring gravitates towards expected levels.

payload.prompt: What is the best approach to reading a match?

options.text: Trust only the stats, ignore what you saw
Use stats and watching to build a full picture
The eye test is always right, stats mislead

explanation.correct: Exactly. Stats answer 'what happened'; watching answers 'how and why'. The best analysis uses both.
explanation.incorrect: Neither stats nor eye test alone tells the full story. Data removes bias; watching captures context and moments.
explanation.sayThisLine: The data says he's great but the eye test disagrees.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The stats say we played well but we felt like we lost control.

payload.question: What is she identifying?

options.text: Stats are always wrong
Stats measure one thing, feeling another; both matter
Her team was overrated
Numbers don't capture the rhythm and momentum

payload.translation: The stats (xG, possession, progressive passes) might support the team's performance, but the emotional experience was different. Both observations are valid.

followUps.line: Which periods did you feel we lost control?
Did a particular substitution change how the match felt?
followUps.why: Connects feeling to a tactical moment.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The eye test captures flow and atmosphere; data captures underlying quality. Neither replaces the other. Combine them.

payload.prompt: Match the stat to what it reveals.

pairs.definition: A team's average points per match over a period, showing consistency independent of number of games played.
A dribble that moves the ball meaningfully towards goal, measuring ball-carrying skill.
The number of shots that force a save or go in, hinting at finishing quality and shot selection.

explanation.summary: Numbers isolate skills: carries show dribbling, shots on target show composure in the box, PPG shows consistency.
explanation.sayThisLine: Look at their shots on target; they're clinical, it's not luck.

payload.prompt: A team is averaging 2.1 points per game in the last 5 but the last match 'felt sloppy'. What's the smartest take?

options.text: The stats are wrong, they are regressing
Ignore the feeling and trust the recent PPG
Good form with one ugly win is still form; watch next match to confirm

explanation.correct: Smart. 2.1 PPG over 5 matches is good; one sloppy win doesn't erase that. But watch the next game to see if sloppiness is a pattern.
explanation.incorrect: Numbers show output (points), not quality. One ugly win doesn't cancel recent good form, but you should check if it becomes a trend.

exchanges.theirMessage: Our new striker has 2 goals in 4 games. We're not sure he's the right fit.

replies.text: What's his xG? If it's low, he's just having a quiet run.
replies.theirResponse: Actually, 1.8 xG so he's slightly underperforming. That's reassuring.
replies.coachNote: You're reading between the stats and the feeling. Smart question.

replies.text: Just wait, strikers need time to settle.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, but how many games? Two or twenty?
replies.coachNote: Vague comfort is weak. Better to ask about the numbers.

replies.text: He looks lost in your system, the finishing will come.
replies.theirResponse: That's bluffing. You haven't watched us play.
replies.coachNote: Avoid guessing what you don't know. Stick to what you can see or ask.

exchanges.theirMessage: The stats say we're playing well but every match is a fight. I'm exhausted.

replies.text: Good form is tough form sometimes. How's the defensive record?
replies.theirResponse: Only 8 goals in 5, so yeah, we're solid at the back.
replies.coachNote: You're validating the stats while acknowledging the grind. Both are real.

replies.text: The stats don't matter if you're not enjoying it.
replies.theirResponse: True, but my team's got a shot at the title, so I'll suffer.
replies.coachNote: Neutral. You're validating the emotion but adding perspective.

replies.text: You need to trust the process and ignore how you feel.
replies.theirResponse: That sounds hollow. Feeling matters too.
replies.coachNote: You're dismissing her experience. The eye test is valid even if the stats are positive.

payload.prompt: Complete the balanced view.
payload.template: Stats show {{what_stats}} while watching shows {{what_watch}}, so the full picture uses {{how}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Numbers isolate quality independent of luck and emotion; watching reveals context and flow. Together they tell the story.
explanation.incorrect: One-dimensional analysis misses the sport. Numbers and eye test answer different questions.
